essentialQuestion.source: How can a computer learn from examples, and why do the examples matter?
essentialQuestion.back: How can a computer learn from examples, and why are the examples important?

learningGoal.source: Train a tiny model with labelled examples, and explain why relevant, correctly labelled examples and fair tests matter.

read.sections.0.heading.source: A model learns from labelled examples
read.sections.0.heading.back: A model learns from labelled examples

read.sections.0.text.source: Some AI learns a bit like studying with flashcards. At Sunrise Garden, people collected training data: pictures of leaves, each with the correct answer, called a label, either “healthy” or “sick”. The computer uses these examples to build a model. It uses the model to predict the label of a leaf it has never seen. This is machine learning. Nobody writes the rule “spots mean sick”; the computer finds patterns like that in the examples. Learning from labelled examples is called supervised learning, one kind of machine learning. It is an old idea. A machine called the perceptron learned from marked cards in 1958, and researchers studied this lesson's method in 1967. It became far more useful after 2010, with more data and faster computers.
read.sections.0.text.back: Some AI learns in a way a bit like studying with flashcards. At Sunrise Garden, people collected training data: pictures of leaves, each with the correct answer, called a label, either “healthy” or “sick”. The computer uses these examples to build a model. The computer uses that model to predict the label of a leaf it has never seen. This is machine learning. Nobody writes the rule “spots mean sick”; the computer itself finds patterns like that in the examples. Learning from labelled examples is called supervised learning, one kind of machine learning. This is an old idea. A machine called the perceptron learned from marked cards in 1958, and researchers studied the method in this lesson in 1967. This method became much more useful after 2010, with more data and faster computers.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Supervised learning" as "pembelajaran terawasi", the usual term in Indonesian computing books; "pembelajaran terbimbing" is also used. "Flashcards" as "kartu hafalan" (memorising cards).

read.sections.0.simpler.source: At Sunrise Garden, people collected training data. Each leaf picture has the right answer, called a label: “healthy” or “sick”. The computer uses them to make a model. It uses the model to guess. This is machine learning. Nobody tells it “spots mean sick”. It finds that in the examples. Learning from labels is called supervised learning. It is an old idea. A machine did it in 1958. This method was studied in 1967. It grew more useful after 2010.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: At Sunrise Garden, people collected training data. Every leaf picture has the correct answer, called a label: “healthy” or “sick”. The computer uses them to make a model. The computer uses that model to guess. This is machine learning. Nobody says “spots mean sick”. The computer finds it by itself in the examples. Learning from labels is called supervised learning. This is an old idea. A machine did it in 1958. This method was studied in 1967. This method became more useful after 2010.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Test the model with new examples
read.sections.1.heading.back: Test the model with new examples

read.sections.1.text.source: To find out whether a model works, you test it with new leaves it did not learn from. The first model learned from only two examples, a big dark green leaf and a brown leaf with spots. It guesses in a simple way: it finds the example most similar to the new leaf and copies its label. It got four of six new leaves right. It called a small, light green leaf “sick” and a yellow leaf with no spots “healthy”. The model was not broken. It had too few examples to compare with.
read.sections.1.text.back: To find out whether a model works, you test it with new leaves that it did not learn from. The first model learned from only two examples, a big dark green leaf and a brown spotted leaf. This model guesses in a simple way: it looks for the example most like the new leaf, then copies its label. The model guessed four of six new leaves correctly. The model called a small light green leaf “sick” and a yellow leaf without spots “healthy”. The model was not broken. It had too few examples to compare with.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Then you test the model on leaves it has not seen. The first model had only two examples. One was dark green. One was brown with spots. It finds the example most like the new leaf. It copies its label. It got four of six right. It called a small new leaf “sick” and a yellow leaf “healthy”. It had too few examples.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Then you test the model with leaves it has never seen. The first model had only two examples. One was dark green. One was brown with spots. The model looks for the example most like the new leaf. The model copies its label. The model was right on four of six. The model called a small newly grown leaf “sick” and a yellow leaf “healthy”. Its examples were too few.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Better examples help, but tests have limits
read.sections.2.heading.back: Better examples help, but testing has limits

read.sections.2.text.source: Next, the team added four more examples, including a small new leaf and a yellow leaf with no spots. Now the model got all six new leaves right. Then the team tested two long, thin, striped leaves from a different plant. Both were healthy, but the model called them “sick”, because none of its examples looked similar. After the team added two striped examples, it got them right. Relevant examples with correct labels help. More examples alone do not always help, because a wrong label can make guesses worse. And a small test cannot prove the model will work on every new plant.
read.sections.2.text.back: Next, the team added four more examples, including a small newly grown leaf and a yellow leaf without spots. Now the model guessed all six new leaves correctly. Then the team tested two long, slim, striped leaves from another plant. Both were healthy, but the model called them “sick”, because none of its examples looked similar. After the team added two striped leaf examples, the model guessed them correctly. Suitable examples with correct labels help. More examples alone do not always help, because one wrong label can make guesses worse. And a small test cannot prove that the model will work for every new plant.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Next, the team added four more examples. Now it got all six right. Then the team tried a new plant with long, striped leaves. They are healthy, but the model said “sick”. No example looked like them. The team added two striped leaves. Then it got them right. Good examples with the right labels help. More examples alone do not always help. A wrong label can make it worse. A small test cannot prove it works on every new plant.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Next, the team added four more examples. Now the model was right on all six. Then the team tried a new plant with long striped leaves. Those leaves are healthy, but the model said “sick”. No example was like them. The team added two striped leaves. Then the model guessed them correctly. Good examples with correct labels help. More examples alone do not always help. A wrong label can make it worse. A small test cannot prove the model works for every new plant.

watch.summary.source: This video explains computer vision. Computer vision is how a computer finds meaning in pictures. A computer does not see a picture like you do. It sees a number for each tiny dot of colour. Writing exact rules for a shape, like the letter X, does not work well, because people draw an X in many ways. With machine learning, the computer learns from many labelled examples instead. It is like learning with flashcards. The computer guesses, checks the answer and slowly gets better. Harder pictures, like faces, need bigger models. The video shows farm robots that tell crops from weeds. It also warns about a problem. If the training data leaves some people out, the tool can fail for them. So training data must be large and varied.
watch.summary.back: This video explains computer vision. Computer vision is how a computer finds meaning in pictures. A computer does not see a picture like you. A computer sees one number for each very small dot of colour. Writing exact rules for a shape, like the letter X, does not work well, because people draw an X in many ways. With machine learning, the computer learns from many labelled examples. This is like learning with flashcards. The computer guesses, checks the answer, and slowly becomes better. Harder pictures, like faces, need bigger models. The video shows farm robots that tell crops from weeds. The video also warns about a problem. If the training data does not include some people, the tool can fail for them. So training data must be large and varied.

educatorNotes.1.source: The model in the activity is deliberately simple: a nearest-neighbour model (k = 1) that copies the label of the most similar example. It is one supervised method; Cover and Hart's 1967 paper studied this rule, and Rosenblatt's perceptron, shown in July 1958, also learned from labelled examples. Real AI is far bigger, and other kinds of machine learning don't need a label on every example, but the points about examples and testing are the same.
educatorNotes.1.back: The model in this activity is made simple on purpose: a nearest-neighbour model (k = 1) that copies the label from the most similar example. It is one supervised learning method; Cover and Hart's 1967 paper studied this rule, and Rosenblatt's perceptron, shown in July 1958, also learned from labelled examples. Real AI is much bigger, and other kinds of machine learning don't need a label on every example, but the points about examples and testing stay the same.
educatorNotes.1.note: "Nearest-neighbour model" as "model tetangga terdekat", as the activity's interface (digitalWorld.trainModel.how3).
